explanation: Tipping is not part of mainland Chinese restaurant culture; menu prices are final and there is no built-in service charge being pointed to. Staff may refuse a tip outright or chase you down to return it, and some locals read an offered tip as implying they're underpaid, though this isn't universally seen as outright insulting. The real exceptions are tour guides and drivers, who commonly expect a tip, and a handful of international luxury hotels catering to Western guests.
local_tip: Skip tipping at everyday restaurants, but set aside a modest cash tip for a tour guide or driver at the end of a trip, since that's the one context where it's genuinely expected.
regional_note: Hong Kong and Macau, shaped by longer British and Portuguese influence, have normalized tipping (often ~10%) far more than mainland China.

also_check.note: Tipping is not practiced and can be seen as confusing or even insulting; excellent service is simply the norm.
Tipping 15-20% at restaurants is standard and service staff rely on it as part of their income.
A service charge is legally included in the bill, but rounding up or leaving small change is a nice gesture.
